title: When something goes wrong
job: Problems, asking for help, complaining calmly
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE THING NEEDED IS THE SUBJECT, and this is the module's best rule because English hides it completely. Mne núzhen bilét, Mne nuzhná pómoshch', Mne núzhno vrémya — núzhen agrees with the THING, and the person sits in the dative. "I need a ticket" has the person as subject and shows none of it. This is M1's dative frame with agreement switched on, and it is where Russian's habit of putting the person in an oblique case stops being a curiosity.

U menyá bolít golová is the same habit again: the body part is the SUBJECT — bolít agrees with it, bolyát for two — and the person is in the genitive after u, exactly as in L1-M8's u menyá yest'. Three constructions, one shape: the person is never the subject of their own need, their own having, or their own pain.

The past tense agrees with the SUBJECT, which L1-M5 taught with kupíl and kupíla. A problem report drills it at length: Ya poteryál said by a man, Ya poteryála by a woman — and On poteryál, Oná poteryála when the subject is someone else. It is the subject, not the speaker; those coincide only when the subject is ya.

COMPLAINING RUNS THE OPPOSITE WAY FROM ENGLISH. Russian complains directly, and the hedged English complaint — "I'm afraid there seems to be a small problem" — reads as evasive rather than as polite. What carries politeness is M1's frame in front and then a plain statement: Izviníte, pozháluysta, u menyá probléma. A learner who softens a Russian complaint the English way will not be understood as polite.

núzhen, nuzhná and núzhno are one word's cells and share M1's row, because they are not aspect partners — choosing between them is choosing what the thing needed is, not how an action is presented. That is M6's test running again.

sentences.cue: Excuse me, I have a problem

words.note: Feminine. Note there is no yest' — u menyá probléma, not u menyá yest' probléma, because a problem is not a possession.
A whole surface, and the one hedge Russian does use. It reports a fact regretfully; it does not soften a demand.

sentences.trap: The politeness is entirely in izviníte, and after it the statement is flat. Softening the problem itself is what makes an English speaker sound evasive here.
sentences.sound: iz-vi-NI-tye u mi-NYA pra-BLYE-ma. The o of probléma reduces to a, so the word starts pra-.

variations.changed: without the opener — abrupt, but not rude
the one hedge the language uses
M1's other opener

mistake.why: A problem is not a possession: u menyá probléma.

sentences.usage: Opening any complaint — at a counter, a hotel desk, an office.

words.note: The masculine cell of M1's núzhno. It agrees with the THING needed — bilét — and not with the person, who is in the dative.
The feminine cell, stressed on the ending. Mne nuzhná pómoshch' — help is feminine, so the word for "needed" is too.

sentences.trap: Which form to use is decided by what is NEEDED. A man saying Mne nuzhná pómoshch' is right, and a woman saying Mne núzhen bilét is right — the speaker's own gender never enters it.
sentences.sound: mnye NU-zhyn bi-LYET. The zh is hard, which pulls the e after it back towards y.

variations.changed: a feminine thing needed
a neuter thing — M1's original cell
a question, and a different person in the dative

mistake.why: pómoshch' is feminine, so: Mne nuzhná pómoshch'.

sentences.usage: Saying what you need. The commonest sentence at any counter.
sentences.mnemonic: It agrees with the thing, never with you.

words.note: Feminine, ending in a consonant plus a soft sign — after M2's mat' and doch', M4's ploshchad' and M5's sol'. The ending never says the gender.

sentences.trap: Two words agree with pómoshch' here and neither of them is a verb: nuzhná and vásha. The noun is running the whole sentence from the end of it.
sentences.sound: mnye nuzh-NA VA-sha PO-mashch'. The shch is one long soft sound, as in M5's ugoshcháytes'.

variations.changed: without saying whose
the offer, which is what a stranger says
a masculine thing, so both words move

mistake.why: The person needing goes in the dative: Mne nuzhná vásha pómoshch'.

sentences.usage: Asking for real help rather than a small favour — M1's pomogíte is for the small ones.
sentences.mnemonic: The noun runs the sentence from the end.

words.note: It agrees with the body part, not with the person: bolít for one, bolyát for two. The person is in the genitive after u, as in L1-M8's u menyá yest'.
End-stressed in the nominative and stem-stressed in the accusative — the stress moves, and the mark is the only thing that records it.

sentences.trap: The head is doing the hurting and you are merely where it is happening. That is the third construction in this course built on the same habit, after u menyá yest' and Mne núzhen.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA ba-LIT ga-la-VA. Four unstressed o's in a row, all reduced to a, and only the last syllable of each word carries.

variations.changed: two of them, so the verb goes plural
a different person, in the genitive
one of them, so the verb goes back to the singular

mistake.why: The person goes after u in the genitive: U menyá bolít golová.

sentences.usage: At a doctor's, or as a reason for going home early.
sentences.mnemonic: The pain is the subject. You are the place.

words.note: One word for the leg and the foot; Russian does not split them. The stress moves between singular and plural, which is common in this class of noun.

sentences.trap: nogá and nógi differ only in where the stress falls — and that difference is singular against plural, which is why the mark is not decoration.
sentences.sound: u mi-NYA ba-LYAT NO-gi. The plural pulls the stress onto the first syllable, the reverse of the singular.

variations.changed: a different person

variations.script: У меня болит голова и болят ноги
variations.cue: My head aches and my legs hurt
variations.changed: both, and each verb agrees separately
a question about someone else

mistake.why: Two legs take the plural verb: U menyá bolyát nógi.

sentences.usage: After a day of walking, which in a Russian city is most days.
sentences.mnemonic: One hurts, two hurt — the verb counts them.

words.note: The past agrees with the SUBJECT. When the subject is ya that means the speaker, but On poteryál is a man whoever is telling it.
The feminine past, the same -a L1-M5 put on kupíla. Russian has no separate perfect, so this covers "lost" and "have lost" alike.

sentences.trap: Russian has no "have lost". This one past covers both, and the situation says which English would use — which is why the cue here is a perfect and the literal is not.
sentences.sound: ya pa-ti-RYAL bi-LYET. Both o and e of poteryál reduce, so only the last syllable is fully sounded.

variations.changed: said by a woman
someone else, and the past agrees with him
a woman as the subject

mistake.why: The past agrees with the subject: Oná poteryála telefón.

sentences.usage: At a lost-property desk, or explaining why you cannot board.
sentences.mnemonic: The past agrees with the subject, not the speaker.

words.note: L1-M1's verb for a person having a job, doing a second job here for a machine functioning. One word, two uses, and its row stays L1's.
A past with -sya on it — "broke itself", which is how Russian avoids naming who broke it. The reflexive system is L3's; this arrives as a word.

sentences.trap: The verb comes first. Ne rabótayet telefón puts the fault in front and the thing after it, which is the neutral order for reporting something wrong — Telefón ne rabótayet is fine too, and sounds more like an answer than a report.
sentences.sound: nye ra-BO-ta-yit ti-li-FON. The ne is unstressed and leans onto the verb.

variations.changed: the other order — an answer rather than a report
a different thing
broken rather than merely not working

mistake.why: The verb has to be finite: Telefón ne rabótayet.

sentences.usage: Reporting a fault. Said plainly, and heard as plain.
sentences.mnemonic: One verb for a job and for a machine.

sentences.cue: Unfortunately, the car has broken down

words.note: One syllable, so no stress mark. It is the thing most often reported broken in a Russian block of flats.

sentences.trap: slomálas' is feminine because mashína is, and the -sya has become -s' after a vowel. That is a spelling rule of the reflexive ending and not a different word.
sentences.sound: k sa-zha-LYE-ni-yu ma-SHY-na sla-MA-las'. The k is a single consonant with no vowel, attached to the front of the next word.

variations.changed: without the hedge
not working rather than broken
masculine, and a time

sentences.usage: Explaining why you are late or why something cannot happen.
sentences.mnemonic: The thing broke itself. Nobody is named.

sentences.display: Pomogíte mne, pozháluysta, u menyá probléma
sentences.script: Помогите мне, пожалуйста, у меня проблема
sentences.cue: Please help me, I have a problem
sentences.literal: Help to-me, please, at me problem

words.note: The working word for a doctor. L1-M2's dóktor exists but is mostly how a patient addresses one, not what the job is called.

sentences.trap: M1's request frame and this module's plain statement, in one breath. That is the whole shape of a Russian complaint: the politeness in front, the fact behind.
sentences.sound: pa-ma-GHI-tye mnye pa-ZHA-lsta u mi-NYA pra-BLYE-ma. Two long words, and the pause is at the comma.

variations.cue: Please help, I need a doctor
variations.changed: the need frame instead of the problem
the other opener and the feminine need

mistake.script: Помогите меня, пожалуйста, у меня проблема
mistake.why: pomóch' takes the dative: Pomogíte mne, pozháluysta.

sentences.usage: When something has gone properly wrong and you need a stranger's help.

sentences.cue: I've lost my bag. What should I do?

words.note: Feminine, so the accusative shows: súmku. It covers a handbag, a shopping bag and a rucksack alike.
The imperfective of doing. Chto délat'? is a fixed question with no subject — the same shape as M7's Chto peredát'?

sentences.trap: Chto délat'? has no "should" and no "I" in it, and it is not a rhetorical question. It is what a Russian actually asks when they want to be told the next step.
sentences.sound: ya pa-ti-RYA-la SUM-ku. shto DYE-lat'? The second half is two words and both are short.

variations.cue: I've lost my bag. What should I do?
variations.changed: said by a man
a masculine object — the verb does not care

variations.cue: I have a problem. What should I do?
variations.changed: the problem frame in front of it

mistake.why: The thing lost is an object: Ya poteryála súmku.

sentences.usage: At a police station, a lost-property office, or to anyone standing nearby.
sentences.mnemonic: Chto délat'? — no subject, and a real question.
